title: Can a marketer prepare customer interviews without doing the final video edit?
summary: Help a marketing team turn customer interviews into a useful source brief and selects handoff, without locking the editor into a finished rough cut.
body_markdown:
## What you’ll take away


- Give the editor a question and source candidates, not only a rewritten script.
- Separate required facts from suggested creative choices.
- Keep full source context available so the editor can improve the story.


## Start with the decision marketing owns


Marketing should identify the audience, the use of the video, and the question it must answer. Those choices guide the edit more than a generic request for a “strong customer story.” Make the intended result specific enough that an editor can reject irrelevant material.


In an illustrative brief, the team needs a video explaining how a customer introduced a new review process. The marketing contribution is knowing that implementation confidence matters to the campaign. It is not deciding every cut before anyone has watched how the customer delivers the answer.


## Prepare readable source material


Point a Wideframe chat at the approved interview recordings. The[export-transcript recipe](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/export-transcript/) provides a starting point for readable, timecoded material. Use the public recipe to add the task, then specify the files and the form the producer will read.


A transcript lets a marketer identify promising passages, but do not judge solely from words on a page. A sentence may depend on the question, include a difficult visual cut, or sound different from how it reads. Keep the editor's access to the original recording central to the handoff.


## Find candidate answers rather than writing new testimony


Ask for passages that answer the campaign question, and keep the customer's wording. Write your own short notes explaining relevance, but distinguish those notes from quotations. A polished marketing summary is a brief, not a source clip.


Choose a small set of strong candidates and useful alternatives. Give the editor enough options to solve pacing or coverage problems without making them reread an unfiltered transcript. If a required point is missing, identify it as a gap instead of writing a sentence the customer never recorded.


## Explain priority without prescribing every cut


Label the essential facts and any passages that must not be used. Treat proposed order, preferred opening, and visual ideas as suggestions unless the brief truly requires them. This lets the editor improve the construction without guessing which decisions are flexible.


A useful note might say, “The pilot limitation must remain, but choose either of these two explanations of setup.” That is clearer than a paper edit that appears locked while its author expects the editor to fix it creatively. Use language that matches the actual authority of the instruction.


## Choose the handoff format together


Ask whether the editor wants a source-linked document, markers, or a separate selects sequence. Wideframe's[Premiere workflow](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/export-premiere/) supports an editable source-based handoff when that is useful. Keep the source folder organization and access arrangements clear.


If the editor wants to hear the answers in context, add and save[Stringout for Review](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/stringout-for-review/) in a blank Wideframe chat. Invoke it on the agreed interview sources with the buyer topics to mark. Its speech-based sequence preserves usable spoken runs in source order and calls for a project plus review MP4. Agree on its silence and minimum-take thresholds before using the reel as the review scope; it is not the final story order.


Do not send only a flattened preview when the editor needs to extend a quote or replace a take. A review video may help communicate the idea, but it should accompany rather than replace the editable materials required for the job.


## Keep feedback tied to the brief


When the editor returns a cut, review whether it answers the intended question and represents the customer accurately. Explain concerns in those terms before suggesting arbitrary timing changes. “The setup effort is unclear” tells the editor what needs solving; “make the first section ten seconds shorter” may remove the only explanation.


Once the changes are concrete, provide notes against the correct version. Keep one person responsible for resolving conflicting marketing feedback. The assistant can help implement defined revisions, but it cannot choose the campaign's priority on behalf of competing stakeholders.


## Make the next handoff familiar


Reuse the same simple brief structure: audience question, intended use, required facts, candidate sources, exclusions, and open questions. Let the actual customer story change. Over time, the editor can tell marketing which preparation helps and which creates redundant work.


This gives marketing a productive role in footage preparation without requiring it to become the finishing department. The repeated Wideframe job is finding and organizing relevant material; the ongoing collaboration is deciding how to turn it into a useful film.
